item.title: If You’re a Woman of a Certain Age, Beware the Risk of HPV
item.description:
Aging

If You’re a Woman of a Certain Age, Beware the Risk of HPV

An old/new sexual scourge is on the rise, and older women should be aware.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Human papilloma virus, or HPV, is not only a problem of the young.
  • HPV can lie dormant for decades and is easy to contract anew.
  • Medical guidelines recommend discontinuing pap smears at age 65 if they’ve been negative for 10 years.
  • If you’re sexually active, you may want to reconsider that recommendation.
Source: Vlada Karpovich/Pexels

Baby Boomers came of age during the Sexual Revolution and learned something both older and younger American cohorts missed: how not to use a condom. Between the invention of the birth control pill in 1960 and the AIDS epidemic in the 1980s, many then-young and now-older adults “learned” to have sex without condoms or fear of pregnancy.

Now, a recent study in BMJ Global Oncology found that women aged 65 and over had the most rapidly rising rates of Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) of any age cohort—and HPV causes more than 90 percent of cervical cancers.

Current pap smear guidelines recommend stopping pap smears altogether in women aged 65 or older with a ten-or-so-year history of normal paps. Stopping is recommended even if, decades before, a woman had abnormal results and/or HPV.

As ever-growing numbers of women live beyond 65, however, there are several things you may want to consider regarding paps and HPV:

  • HPV, often dubbed “the common cold of sexual activity” has, does, or will affect about 80-85% of all sexually active women (and 90% of sexually active men) during their lifetimes.
  • The virus has multiple strains, some more implicated in cervical cancer than others. Pap smears detect HPV and can identify which strain(s) are present.
  • HPV generally leaves no visible symptoms (with the exception of genital warts, caused by lower risk strains of HPV), and can spread easily without knowing you carry it.
  • HPV spreads through skin-to-skin contact, not semen or vaginal fluids. This means it can spread without penetrative sex.
  • HPV can lie dormant for decades. The fact that it’s increasing most rapidly in women over 65 is probably due to a number of factors: lower condom use in this age group, dormant viruses “waking up” decades after initial infection, lack of HPV vaccinations, and other factors we don’t completely understand.
  • Vaccines are highly effective for HPV and can be used even if one already has HPV—vaccines can protect against other strains of the virus a person does not have—but are not approved or recommended for adults over 60.
  • A BMJ Global Oncology study of more than 2 million women found found that almost 14 percent of women over 65 had higher rates of severe HPV cervical changes (compared to less than 9 percent in younger women). This further puts older women at greater risk for cervical cancer from HPV.

If you think you may be at risk for HPV, a pap smear will give you the information you need. If your provider doesn’t recommend a pap smear because you’re over 65, let them know you’d like one anyway. If they resist, it may be time to find another provider—one you feel comfortable discussing sexual behavior with and one who makes you feel heard and respected.

Source: mariakray/Shutterstock

And if you’re over 65 and have been or will be sexually active with a new partner, it may be time to learn to use condoms. (Learning new skills in older adulthood is good for our brains, as well as our bodies.) If condoms are a bridge too far (pun intended), one alternative is to get tested for HPV and ask any new partner to do the same. And if you do have HPV, don’t despair: HPV can be managed, monitored, and treated, and treatments are becoming easier and more effective all the time.

item.title: How to Date Someone With Mental Illness
item.description:
Relationships

How to Date Someone With Mental Illness

Advice from an expert on relationships involving mental illness.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Dating with a serious mental illness can come with stigma and hardship, but it doesn't have to.
  • A successful relationship with serious mental illness falls on maintaining independence and responsibility.
  • Long-term success depends on respecting one's coping skills and routines involving mental illness.

Stigma against dating people with serious mental illness (SMI) is abundant. There is no shortage of discrimination against people who are difficult to understand, whether it be in the workplace or the public sphere, and when bringing them into one’s personal life.

Dating someone with SMI can bring fear and hesitation due to the uncertainty of how a person handles their SMI. But what if we had the tools and wisdom to help us navigate lives that may be “tougher” than the average?

Lauren Elise Rogers is a Certified Holistic Sexuality Educator and Embodied Intimacy & Relationship Coach, known for her warm, approachable style and evidence-informed practice. Grounded in a biopsychosocial model of care, she takes an interdisciplinary approach to sexual and relational challenges, frequently collaborating with clients and their healthcare providers to support comprehensive, individualized care. She helps empower individuals and couples to explore complex topics with curiosity, agency, and confidence.

Sarah An Myers: Dating someone with a serious mental illness like bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, major depressive disorder, or schizophrenia can be daunting. What are some things we can do to either dispel stigma or relieve the pressure on both parties?

Lauren Elise Rogers: Whether we are dating someone with a SMI or dating as a person with a serious mental illness, I believe that we are required to take responsibility for our own embodied experience rather than giving away or taking away responsibilities from the other. Kai Cheng Thom refers to the Ecological Model of Attachment as “one that includes complex and deeply rooted kinship networks, relationships with culture and cultural artifacts, as well as connection to the non-human world.” I like to explain this model to my clients as simply “not putting all of our eggs in the partnership basket.” When dating, we should not be looking for a parent; we should be looking for a partner. We are not meant to do relationships alone. We can allow ourselves to have a team around us, regardless of our mental health status. Approaching relationships with radical honesty, a supportive community, and a team of professionals should be the norm, not the exception. We are all deserving of intimacy and affection! The belief that romantic and sexual relationships should only exist between humans without serious mental illness is discriminatory.

SM: Is your advice the same for those who have never had anyone to take care of them? For example, people who have never had families, parents, siblings, or relatives do the "caretaking" role in both financial and emotional care?

LER: There is no shame in going through a stage of dating that’s more about caretaking than loving. When we haven’t been taken care of in childhood, we will seek out caretaking. This is not “wrong.”

Yet, I’d argue that romantic relationships are not the solution to our perceived lack of wholeness. To enter relationships from such a strong place of need is to entrust another person with too much power. Dené Logan, couples therapist, says that when we make them responsible for healing our original wounds, “we project onto them the fantasy of being the key to our sense of fulfillment.” Then, if/when they decide to cease or change their form of caretaking, the initial “love” we felt disappears, sending us reeling back into the idea that we are unlovable and unworthy. Logan goes on to ask if we are “truly looking to love another person, or to fill the hole within us created by the caregivers and the society who didn’t love us and see us in the ways we longed to be loved and seen"?

Instead of looking to romantic partners to heal the wounds left by our original caregivers, I suggest friendship. Robert Firestone, in his book, The Fantasy Bond: Structure of Psychological Defenses, writes, ”The therapeutic value of friendship must be emphasized, for it is virtually a necessity to share one’s struggle with others who support one’s individuality and personal freedom.”

SM: How does a prospective non-mentally ill partner approach someone with mental illness in the initial stages of dating, and what can they consider when merging their life with that person?

LER: I encourage non-mentally ill partners to approach a prospective mentally-ill partner with patience and spaciousness in the initial stages of dating. During the “honeymoon” stage, in the pure desire for togetherness, couples often sub-consciously detach from their communities and cease the practices that stabilize them when outside of the relationship. They might forego things like movement, therapy, hobbies, nutrition, etc. When considering dating someone with an SMI, non-mentally ill individuals can support and celebrate pre-existing practices that contribute to self-assuredness and self-security. This may look like going slow and spacing out dates to allow for other critical supports to remain, yet it sets the tone and gives both parties a clearer idea of what it could look like to merge lives and support the mentally-ill partner from a place of interdependence rather than co-dependence.

While it may feel like you’re fighting cultural scripts that celebrate enmeshment and spending every moment together, a 2016 study found that folks in interdependent relationships gained strength from knowing that they could each live their own lives and pursue personal goals with the support and encouragement of their partner.

SM: What do both parties have to realistically consider when involving someone with a mental illness in a relationship?

LER: When involving someone with a mental illness, all parties must consider their own limits and capacities. The non-mentally ill partner should be mindful that caretaking is not the same as loving. It is well documented that folks in long-term relationships often feel desire drain when burdened by emotional caretaking. Love does not require us to disappear. It is beautiful and healthy to enforce generative boundaries. Adrienne maree brown, writer, activist, and facilitator, coined two statements that I adore:

  1. “It sounds like you might need some professional support. I love our relationship and don’t want to slip into an inappropriate role of healer or coach here. How can I help you connect to support?”

  2. “There is my work, your work, and our work. I am down for us to do our work, and I will hold down my work, but I cannot take on your work. I deeply support you in figuring out what you need to do around that.”

The partner with SMI can take pride and honor in their domain. Betty Martin, author of The Wheel of Consent, says that a “domain is all that we have a right to and a responsibility for. The more we take responsibility for our domain, the more freedom we have.” SMI is a sacred responsibility that the mentally ill partner has a right to and a responsibility for. Normal is a myth! There are many ways to love, desire, please, and be pleased! You do not move from broken to normal to perfect. All humans are in a continual cycle of woundedness to healing. You are fully enough–right now.

SM: Have you found hope and success with couples in long-term partnerships where serious mental illness does not limit them from a thriving partnership?

LER: Of course! When the partnership is not the sole source of support but rather a piece of the whole support system, I have seen long-term relationships thrive! In her book, Come Together: The Science (and Art!) of Creating Lasting Sexual Connections, Emily Nogaski says, “Confidence is knowing what is true…and joy is loving what is true.” When individuals and partners boldly acknowledge the presence of serious mental illness in their relationships, I find that they confidently lean on their community supports and joyfully celebrate their differences. This type of honesty builds trust and trust is essential to a strong and lasting relationship.

Healthy relationships do not require perfect humans, but simply curious human beings who admire each other and believe in the effort it takes to repair wounds and continually write courageous and radically loving relational scripts.

item.title: Why We Need Community as Much as Friends to Stay Connected
item.description:
Friends

Why We Need Community as Much as Friends to Stay Connected

Personal Perspective: How community brings rootedness to our lives.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Community is based in a shared purpose, place, time, or way of thinking.
  • Friends and community relations offer different kinds of needed social connection.
  • Community connection provides security, belonging, ballast, self-definition, and warmth.

For most people, school is our first community. After school, it’s probably work. Whether you’re a shopkeeper, programmer, or lawyer, you often find community – looser or tighter – with people in your office or who do the same work nearby. Nurses might belong to a union while project managers or HR employees join their professional organizations. It seems obvious.

Looking back, I see that the colleges where I taught English over the years were communities, but that wasn’t obvious to me. I thought of other faculty as co-workers rather than relations. I knew they weren’t friends, though some did become dear friends. I wish I’d have seen them then as I now do – as members of my community, or one significant one. Maybe I would have paid more attention and valued those connections more. Maybe I’d have noticed how my office neighbors brightened my day, more so as I got to know them better and asked about their Cancun vacation or listened to their advice about my injured foot. I wish I’d have brought my home-made lemon bars sometimes, or had been enthusiastic about the department’s whale-watching excursion. Maybe, back then, I’d have discovered the importance of community. But the concept of community eluded me, as I imagine it might for others.

I knew that friendship was something to cherish and a powerful source of connection. It had a familiar and familial feel, like a natural bond with two or three people who formed islands we inhabited together and ranged across areas of intensity and playfulness, adventure and tenderness. Community is quite different but it offers something else that helps us thrive: a sense of belonging and security.

I think we’re fundamentally pack animals, like dogs or wolves or zebras needing to be part of a companion group that situates us inside its protective boundaries. It’s like a larger, social version of family (our original pack) that provides another powerful connection. It’s not the private, intimate and more binding friendship kind, but the kind that connects our public selves to others just enough to function as a unit with a shared purpose, place, time, or way of thinking. It’s this community connection with people who are neither strangers nor friends but something in between that can make us feel recognized, accepted, valued, and even – in their reflection and feedback – better defined. Community can feel like ballast, something that’s there despite any one person in it. In fact, it’s considered such an important component of happiness that an entire discipline within psychology is devoted to its study, and The Journal of Community Psychology to papers on the subject.

The importance of community finally dawned on me after living without it for too long. Like everyone, my social orientation got set in motion at home. I didn’t feel I belonged in my original pack. I wasn’t like my mother or my stepfather. My brother, who was a closer fit, is older and, of course, male. I believe that as I moved into one community after another that I didn’t recognize as such, I just reproduced that feeling of not belonging.

School didn’t seem like community. Although I had a random friend here and there, they were mostly other kids who hung back and tried to disappear. Aside from a couple of years when I was swept into junior high school popularity—and found it terribly uncomfortable—I didn’t have boyfriends, didn’t go to dances, and didn’t work on the school newspaper. Bottom line: I was a weirdo loner.

When I went to college, I requested my own room and got it. I went to classes. I studied. I did secretarial work at the law school for spending money. I wasn’t part of any group; I didn’t even understand that there were groups. But by the time I was a junior I was so worn down by my loneliness that I decided to join humanity. But I had to figure out how. First, I made a study of how students managed to find friends and party together, gather for protests, organize projects, and exhibit their artwork. Then I noticed the flyers advertising campus clubs. What a revelation. I investigated and ended up joining a group of political activists. I didn’t quite fit in, but it led to other groups where I did. When I auditioned and got a part in the college play, I had my first experience of community – of near-strangers working in concert to do something together. It was exciting and validating. By the opening-night party, I understood something of the value of community. But I would need more years to learn how to find my communities and cultivate my place in them.

That’s the challenge: Unless your family imprinted it on you, you have to become aware of the need for community and how to find yours. Which is where psychology comes in. It pays to begin with genuine self-inquiry about what you learned from your family about belonging and how you commonly situate yourself in groups. You might question how comfortable you are in them—and if the answer is “not very,” investigate further, maybe with help from a therapist.

Community requires practical considerations, too. Out in the world, community isn’t inevitable. And even when it can be, like at work, you can still feel like an outsider. As I discovered, finding community takes work and introspection. Religion certainly can offer community, but you have to be religious to join. Sports seem to create community for a lot of people, as do certain music groups. Whatever your interests, there are probably groups, like Rotary or dog rescuers or quilters, new parents, or yoga devotees. Once you work out what and how much community you want, you begin to see possibilities everywhere, and if you’re lucky, you also see the trust, camaraderie, warmth, and rootedness they bring to our lives.
